text: Everything from scoping through testing is real and verified -- but right now it all lives in Mara's head and her terminal history. If she's out the week a fifth server needs hardening, none of that knowledge is usable by anyone else. Writing it down is what turns a one-time favor into something the team can actually repeat.

For the hardening side, Mara writes a runbook with one entry per checklist item, each in the same five-part shape: what it is, in plain language; why it matters, the specific risk it closes; how to apply it, the exact command; how to verify it, the exact proof it worked; and who owns re-checking it, and how often.

The Sentinel rule gets its own entry, written so a future analyst understands why the query is shaped the way it is -- the detection target in plain English, the finished KQL itself, the scheduling settings and why lookback is longer than run frequency, and critically, the three test scenarios from last lesson as a ready-made regression test.

A runbook and a changelog are not the same document. The runbook describes what's true right now, on these four servers. A changelog records what changed and when -- applied CIS Level 1, created this Sentinel rule, dated. One answers what's true today; the other answers how it got there.

Hartwell needs both, and conflating them into one document would make each harder to use for its actual purpose -- someone troubleshooting today needs the runbook, someone auditing history needs the changelog.
With the project fully documented, next lesson is the conversation all of this was building toward -- presenting the findings to Dale.
